title: How Python runs & your setup
summary: Understand what happens when you run Python, then install it cleanly and run your first script from the terminal.
objectives: Explain what an interpreter does when it runs your code
Tell the difference between source code, bytecode, and the Python runtime
Install Python and confirm the version from the terminal
Run code two ways: the interactive REPL and a saved .py file
Use a virtual environment to keep project dependencies isolated
Read and understand a basic traceback when something breaks

quiz.q: What does the Python interpreter do with your source code?
options: Translates it once into a standalone .exe
Reads and executes it line by line at run time
quiz.why: Python is interpreted: the interpreter reads your code, compiles it to bytecode, and executes it when you run the program — no separate build step into a standalone binary.

quiz.q: Which command shows the Python version installed on your machine?
quiz.why: python --version (or python -V) prints the interpreter version, which confirms Python is installed and on your PATH.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to use a virtual environment per project?
options: It isolates each project's packages so versions don't clash
It is required to write any Python
quiz.why: A virtual environment keeps each project's dependencies separate, so installing a package for one project never breaks another.

quiz.q: Name the file extension used for a saved Python script.
quiz.why: Python source files end in .py, and you run them with python yourfile.py.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the REPL and when would you use it?
quiz.answer: The REPL is the interactive Python prompt where you type one line and see the result instantly; use it to experiment and test small ideas.
quiz.why: REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop — perfect for quick checks, but real programs live in saved .py files.

quiz.q: When a program crashes, what does the traceback's last line usually tell you?
quiz.answer: The type of error and a short message, such as NameError or ZeroDivisionError, describing what went wrong.
quiz.why: Read tracebacks from the bottom up: the final line names the error and reason, and the lines above show where it happened.

body_markdown:
## What actually happens when you "run" Python

When you run a program, your code has to become instructions the computer can execute. With some languages you **compile** the whole program ahead of time into a standalone file. Python is different: it is **interpreted**. The Python **interpreter** reads your source code, quietly compiles it to an intermediate form called **bytecode**, and then executes that bytecode line by line.

The practical upshot: there is no separate build step. You write a file, you run it, you see the result. That fast feedback loop is one reason Python is so beginner-friendly.

## Source code, bytecode, and the runtime

Think of three layers. Your **source code** is the `.py` text file you write. The interpreter turns it into **bytecode** (you may notice a `__pycache__` folder appear). The **Python runtime** — often called CPython — is the program that actually runs that bytecode on your operating system.

You never write bytecode by hand. Knowing it exists just helps the whole thing stop feeling like magic.

## Installing Python and checking it works

Download the latest Python from python.org and install it. The single most important check is that your terminal can find it.

```bash
python --version
# Python 3.12.4
```

If that prints a version number, Python is installed and on your **PATH**. On some systems you type `python3` instead of `python`.

## Two ways to run code

The first way is the **REPL** — the interactive prompt. Type `python`, and you get a `>>>` prompt where each line runs instantly. Great for experiments.

```python
>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> print("Hello")
Hello
```

The second way is a **saved script**. Put your code in a file and run the file. This is how real programs are written.

```bash
# hello.py contains:  print("Hello, world!")
python hello.py
# Hello, world!
```

## Virtual environments: one clean box per project

Different projects often need different package versions. A **virtual environment** is an isolated copy of Python for a single project, so installing something for one project never breaks another.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
# Windows:
.venv\Scripts\activate
# macOS / Linux:
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Once activated, anything you install with `pip` lives only inside that project. Get into the habit now — every serious project you build will use one.

## Reading errors without panic

When code breaks, Python prints a **traceback**. Read it from the **bottom up**: the last line names the error type and message. Errors are normal and they are information, not failure.

## Your task

Install Python, confirm the version in your terminal, create a virtual environment, then write and run a `hello.py` file that prints your name.

slides.title: How Python runs & your setup
slides.narration: Welcome to Month One of your journey from maths graduate to A I engineer. This very first lesson is about what actually happens when you run Python, and how to set up your machine the right way. By the end you'll understand the interpreter, you'll have Python installed and checked, and you'll have run your first script from the terminal.

slides.title: What is an interpreter?
bullets: Python is interpreted, not compiled ahead of time.
The interpreter reads and runs your code.
No separate build step — write, run, see result.
That fast loop is why Python feels friendly.
slides.narration: Let's start with the big idea. When you run a program, your code has to become instructions the computer can execute. Some languages compile everything ahead of time into one standalone file. Python is different. It's interpreted, which means the interpreter reads your code and runs it directly. There's no separate build step, so you write a file, you run it, and you see the result straight away.

slides.title: Source, bytecode, runtime
bullets: Source code: the .py text you write.
Bytecode: the in-between form Python makes.
Runtime (CPython): runs the bytecode on your OS.
You never write bytecode by hand.
slides.narration: Under the hood there are three layers worth knowing. Your source code is the dot p y file you write. The interpreter quietly turns it into bytecode, an in-between form, and you might notice a cache folder appear because of this. Then the Python runtime, usually called CPython, actually runs that bytecode on your operating system. You never write bytecode yourself; knowing it exists just stops the whole thing feeling like magic.

slides.title: Install & check the version
bullets: Download the latest Python from python.org.
Confirm your terminal can find it.
On some systems you type python3.
slides.narration: Now let's get it on your machine. Download the latest Python from python dot org and install it. The single most important check is that your terminal can actually find Python. Type python space dash dash version. If it prints a version number, you're installed and ready. On some systems, like Mac and Linux, you may need to type python three instead.

slides.title: PATH: how the terminal finds Python
bullets: PATH is a list of folders the terminal searches.
Python's installer can add it for you.
If 'python' isn't found, PATH is usually why.
On Windows, tick 'Add to PATH' when installing.
slides.narration: If you type python and the terminal says it can't find it, the culprit is almost always your PATH. PATH is simply a list of folders your terminal searches when you type a command. The Python installer can add Python to this list for you. On Windows especially, make sure you tick the box that says Add Python to PATH during installation. It saves a lot of confusion later.

slides.title: Run code: the REPL
bullets: Type python to open the interactive prompt.
Each line runs instantly at the >>> prompt.
Perfect for quick experiments and checks.
slides.narration: There are two ways to run Python, and the first is the REPL, the interactive prompt. Just type python on its own and you get three greater-than signs. Now every line you type runs immediately. It's a wonderful playground for testing a small idea or checking how something behaves. REPL, by the way, stands for read, evaluate, print, loop.

slides.title: Run code: a saved script
bullets: Put your code in a file ending in .py.
Run the whole file from the terminal.
This is how real programs are written.
slides.code:
# hello.py
print("Hello, world!")

# in the terminal:
python hello.py
slides.narration: The second way, and the one real programs use, is a saved script. You put your code in a file ending in dot p y, then run that whole file by typing python space the file name. Here our file hello dot p y just prints Hello, world. Run it, and the message appears. From now on, most of your work lives in saved files like this.

slides.title: Virtual environments
bullets: An isolated copy of Python for one project.
Keeps each project's packages separate.
Stops one install from breaking another project.
Build the habit on every project.
slides.code:
python -m venv .venv
# Windows:
.venv\Scripts\activate
# macOS / Linux:
source .venv/bin/activate
slides.narration: Here's a habit that will save you real pain: the virtual environment. Different projects often need different package versions. A virtual environment is an isolated copy of Python just for one project, so installing something for one project never breaks another. You create one with python dash m venv, then activate it. The command differs slightly on Windows versus Mac and Linux, so use the one for your system.

slides.title: Reading errors calmly
bullets: A crash prints a traceback.
Read it from the bottom up.
The last line names the error and reason.
Errors are information, not failure.
slides.narration: Finally, let's talk about errors, because you'll meet plenty. When code breaks, Python prints a traceback. The trick is to read it from the bottom up. That very last line tells you the type of error and a short reason, like ZeroDivisionError, division by zero. Errors are not failure; they're the interpreter telling you exactly what went wrong and where. Treat them as information.

bullets: Python is interpreted: read, compile, run.
Check it with python --version.
Run code via the REPL or a saved .py file.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Python is interpreted: the interpreter reads your code, compiles it to bytecode, and runs it. You confirm your install with python dash dash version. You can run code interactively in the REPL, or properly from a saved dot p y file. And every project gets its own virtual environment. Your task before the next lesson: install Python, confirm the version in your terminal, create a virtual environment, and write a hello dot p y file that prints your name. Great start, and I'll see you in the next lesson.
